The process begins at a Small Company when an order is received. The Sales Department then reviews and decides to either reject or accept the order. If the order is rejected, the process finishes immediately with a rejection outcome.

If the order is accepted, two departments are informed simultaneously to work in parallel. The Storehouse begins processing the part list while the Engineering Department prepares for assembling.

In the Storehouse, after processing the part list, each required part's quantity is checked. Depending on availability, the part is either reserved if in stock or back-ordered if not available. After either reserving or back-ordering a part, the process determines if there are more parts to process. If additional parts remain, the quantity check repeats for the next part. Once all parts have been processed, the Storehouse work is complete.

Meanwhile, the Engineering Department completes its preparation for assembling. Once both the Storehouse has finished processing all parts and the Engineering Department has completed preparations, the two parallel paths synchronize. The Engineering Department then assembles the bicycle.

After assembly is complete, the Sales Department ships the bicycle to the customer, and the process finishes successfully with the order shipped.

The room service process at The Evanstonian Hotel begins when a guest calls room service. The Room-Service Manager takes down the order and then initiates three parallel activities simultaneously: submitting the order ticket to the kitchen, giving the order to the sommelier, and assigning the order to a waiter.

In the Kitchen, the staff prepares the food based on the submitted order ticket. Meanwhile, the Sommelier fetches wine from the cellar and then prepares the alcoholic beverages. At the same time, the assigned Waiter readies a cart and then prepares the nonalcoholic drinks.

Once all three parallel activities are completed—the food is prepared, the alcoholic beverages are ready, and the nonalcoholic drinks are prepared—the process synchronizes. The Waiter then delivers the complete order to the guest room. After delivery, the Waiter returns to the room-service station and finally debits the guest account, concluding the process.

Regardless of whether the claim was approved with payment scheduled or rejected, both paths converge, and the Handling Department sends a letter to the customer communicating the outcome. This letter is received by the Customer, and the process concludes.

The process begins when a company decides to go public. The company then selects the underwriters who will manage the public offering, and this selection is communicated to the underwriters.

Once the underwriters are engaged, they provide procedural and financial advice to guide the company through the process. The underwriters then buy the issue from the company and subsequently resell the issue to the public. Following this, the underwriters prepare a registration statement for SEC approval and formally register the issue with the SEC.

The underwriters then check compliance with blue-sky laws to ensure the offering meets state securities regulations. After confirming compliance, they begin to firm up the issue price and arrange a road show to generate interest. During the road show, the underwriters talk to potential investors to gauge demand and interest in the offering.

Once these marketing efforts are complete, the underwriters receive clearance from the SEC to proceed. They then fix the final issue price based on market conditions and investor feedback. At this point, a decision is made regarding whether there is any reason not to proceed with the offering.

If there is a reason not to proceed, the process ends without completing the public offering. However, if there is no reason to halt the process, the underwriters enter into a firm commitment to buy the stock from the company and then offer the stock to the public, completing the initial public offering process.

If the claimant is insured, the severity of the claim is evaluated. Based on this evaluation, either simple claim forms are sent to the claimant for less severe claims, or complex claim forms are sent for more severe claims.

After the appropriate forms have been sent, the forms are checked for completeness. If the forms are complete, the claim is registered in the Claims Management system, and the process ends successfully.

However, if the forms are incomplete, the claimant is informed to update the forms. Once the updated forms are received, they are checked again for completeness. This cycle of checking forms, informing the claimant of needed updates, and receiving updated forms continues until the forms are complete and the claim can be registered in the system.

Every weekday morning, the process begins by backing up the database. Following this, the system checks the Account Defaulter table for new records.

If new records are found, the CRM system is checked for new returns. If new returns exist, all defaulting accounts and customers are registered manually. The system then checks if the defaulting client codes have been previously advised. If they have not been previously advised, a table of defaulting accounts is produced and sent to account management. After sending the table, or if the client codes were previously advised, the system checks whether this has been completed by the 2:30pm deadline. If the deadline has not been met, an alert is sent to the supervisor regarding the 2:30pm deadline. Regardless of whether the alert was sent, a new defaulting account report is then completed manually.

If no new records were found in the Account Defaulter table, or if no new returns existed in the CRM system, or after completing the new defaulting account report, the process proceeds to check the CRM system for new returns a second time.

If new returns have been filed during this second check, the system reconciles them with the existing account defaulters table. After reconciliation, the system checks whether this has been completed by the 4:00pm deadline. If the deadline has not been met, a message is sent to the supervisor regarding the 4:00pm deadline. The process then concludes regardless of whether the message was sent.

If no new returns were filed during the second CRM check, the process ends directly without requiring reconciliation.

After reconciliation, or if no new returns were filed, the process checks whether this work was completed by the 4:00 pm deadline. If the deadline was missed, a message is sent to the supervisor regarding the 4:00 pm deadline. Whether the message was sent or the deadline was met, the process then concludes.

The process begins when a switch-over request is initiated. The customer transmits their data, which is then received by the Customer Service department within the Company. The customer service representative enters this data into the CRM system and compares it with the internal customer database. The data is then checked for completeness and plausibility.

If errors are found during this check, the representative corrects them based on an error list before proceeding. If no errors are found, the process continues directly. Next, the system determines whether the customer already exists in the database. If the customer is new, a new customer object is created before preparing the contract documents. If the customer already exists, the process moves directly to preparing contract documents for the power supplier switch.

The contract documents undergo an automated check in the CIS system. If issues are detected, the representative analyzes and resolves them, then regenerates the contract documents, which are checked again. Once the documents pass the automated check, a confirmation document is sent to the customer, and simultaneously a request is sent to the grid operator.

The grid operator receives the request and checks it for supplier concurrence. If there is a supplier concurrence issue, the grid operator informs all involved suppliers and demands conflict resolution, then communicates with the old supplier and carries out the termination of the sales agreement. If there is no concurrence issue, the grid operator transmits a response comment back to customer service.

Upon receiving the response, customer service creates a CIS contract. After a 7-day waiting period, the customer makes their decision. The customer reviews the contract details and either withdraws from the switch contract or confirms it. If the customer withdraws, the process ends for customer service with a withdrawal outcome.

If the customer confirms, three activities happen in parallel at the grid operator: power meter data is transmitted to customer service, power meter data is transmitted to the old supplier, and final billing is computed based on the meter data. The final billing is then sent to the old supplier. Once all three parallel activities complete, the process ends for the grid operator.

The old supplier receives the meter data and billing information, creates the final billing, and sends it to the customer, concluding the process for the customer. Meanwhile, customer service imports the meter data into their systems, marking the successful acquisition of a new customer.

The data is then checked for completeness and plausibility. If errors are found, they are corrected based on an error list before proceeding; otherwise, the process continues directly. Next, Customer Service determines whether the customer already exists in the database. If the customer is new, a new customer object is created; if the customer already exists, this step is skipped.

Customer Service then prepares the contract documents, which undergo an automated check. If issues are detected during this check, the team analyzes and resolves the problems, generates the contract documents again, and repeats the automated check. Once the contract documents pass the check successfully, a confirmation document is sent to the customer, and simultaneously a request is sent to the Grid Operator.

The Grid Operator receives the request and checks the switch-over request for supplier concurrence. After transmitting a response comment back to Customer Service, the Grid Operator determines if there is a supplier concurrence issue. If there is concurrence, the Grid Operator informs the involved suppliers and demands conflict resolution, then communicates with the old supplier and terminates the sales agreement with them before proceeding. If there is no concurrence, the process moves forward directly.

Customer Service then creates a CIS contract, and the customer checks the contract details. The customer has three options: withdraw from the switch contract (which ends the process for Customer Service), confirm the contract, or take no action within 7 days. If the customer confirms the contract or the 7-day timer expires, the process splits into parallel paths.

In one path, the Grid Operator transmits power meter data to Customer Service, who imports the meter data into their systems, completing their part of the process. In the parallel path, the Grid Operator transmits power meter data to the Old Supplier, computes the final billing based on the meter data, and sends the final billing to both the Old Supplier and marks the end of the Grid Operator's involvement. The Old Supplier then creates the final billing and sends it to the customer, concluding the process for the customer.

The process begins on the first of each month at Assembler AG, when an order is placed with a supplier. The order is then sent to the supplier, which triggers a communication to the Supplier organization.

Upon receiving the order, the Supplier processes the order and sends an invoice back to Assembler AG. This invoice transmission represents another communication between the two organizations.

Back at Assembler AG, the invoice is received and then processed by a user. Once the invoice processing is complete, the process ends for Assembler AG.

Meanwhile, after the Supplier has processed the order and sent the invoice, their part of the process also concludes.
